title: Different, not ranked
hook: these ways aim at different ends: God, awakening, character, calm

segments.voice: Yesterday, going deeper in one, and Seneca's warning: everywhere means nowhere. Your line was one well, deep. Did you do your one practice, at its time? Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

A marathon, a swim across a lake, and a mountain climb. All three take training, early mornings, sore legs and stubbornness. Someone could line them up and ask which is the best race. It would be a strange question. They aren't three attempts at the same finish line. They end in different places: a tape across a road, a far shore, a summit. On this tour, it's been easy to treat the world's practices as one long race with different running styles. Sit like this, breathe like that, all heading to the same tape. Today slows down and asks a plainer question: what is each one actually for?
screen: `A MARATHON, A SWIM, A CLIMB.` → `NOT THE SAME FINISH LINE.` → `WHAT IS EACH ONE FOR?`

segments.voice: Listen to how the practices describe their own ends, in their own words. In Christian prayer and contemplation, the aim is God. Augustine opens his Confessions speaking to God directly: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The end there is not a calmer mind, though that may come. It is a relationship, rest in God. In the Buddhist Dhammapada, the end has another name. The verses speak of nirvana, the going out of craving, as the highest happiness. That is awakening, and it is described without a creator God at its center. In the Confucian Analects, the aim is different again: becoming a person of noble character, a junzi, through study, ritual courtesy and care for others. The end is a good human being in a good society. And in modern secular practices, like the mindfulness-based therapy this path met last week, the stated aim is often more modest: calm, attention, a lower chance of falling back into depression. Four ends: God, awakening, character, calm. They overlap at the edges. A Christian may grow calmer, a Buddhist kinder, a therapy patient more thoughtful. But each tradition names its own goal, and the respectful thing is to let it. Saying they're different isn't saying one is better. It's saying each deserves to be understood on its own terms, not folded into someone else's. Comparing aims is only description. Ranking them is a different act, and this path doesn't do it.
screen: `GOD: A RESTLESS HEART AT REST.` · `AWAKENING: THE GOING OUT OF CRAVING.` · `CHARACTER: A NOBLE PERSON.` · `CALM: A STEADIER MIND.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT, NOT RANKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note what each aims at. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind your own practice, the one you chose yesterday, or any you keep. Ask it, gently: what are you for? Is it God, if you pray? Awakening? Becoming a better person? A calmer mind? Something else entirely? Don't rush to a neat answer. Let it be more than one thing if it is. Just listen for what your practice is reaching toward. The bell holds the time.
Different. The world's practices aim at different ends, God, awakening, character, calm, and each is understood on its own terms, without a ranking. Today's word.

Your line: different ends. Today, when you hear someone describe their faith or practice, ask them what it's for, and listen to their answer in their own words. Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Traditions describe the aim of practice in their own terms: Christians often speak of union with or rest in God, Buddhists of awakening and nirvana, Confucians of becoming a person of noble character, and secular programs of calm, attention and well-being.

notes: Check the Pusey 1838 wording of Confessions 1.1 against a scan (the sentence begins 'for Thou madest us...').

The Analects references for the junzi are given broadly; a reviewer may want one precise passage. Confirm the pinyin-style pronunciation 'JWUN-dzuh' for 君子 (jūnzǐ).
The script says the aim of Christian prayer and contemplation is God; confirm this general statement.
The mindfulness-based therapy reference points to day 1410 (MBCT); its aim is described as reducing relapse into depression, with no statistic.
The day is built to describe aims without ranking; the fork deliberately rejects both 'all the same' and 'only mine'.
